transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

I guess… what finally made me come in is that I just don’t feel like myself anymore. I keep thinking maybe I’m just tired or in a rut, but it feels bigger than that. I used to make time for things without even thinking about it—painting, hiking on weekends when I could, choir practice, Sunday gatherings with my family—and those were the things that sort of made me feel like me.

Now, even if I have a free hour, I’ll just sit there. I’ll think, “I could get out my paints,” or “I should call and see what everyone’s doing Sunday,” and I just… don’t care enough to move. It’s not that I suddenly hate those things. It’s more like the feeling I used to get from them isn’t there, and I can’t seem to make myself want them. That’s been really unsettling. I suppose that’s why I’m here.
How long have you been feeling this loss of interest in the things you used to enjoy?

It’s been… about eight months, I think. It didn’t happen all at once, which is part of why I kept telling myself it was just stress or being busy. It started building after I took over this STEM-Arts curriculum initiative at work. At first I thought, well, of course I’m drained, it’s a big project, there are a lot of moving pieces, and I was putting so much of myself into making it work.

But then months kept passing, and I realized it wasn’t just that I didn’t have time for painting or hiking or family things. Even when I did have time, I didn’t feel drawn to them anymore. So… yes, I’d say around eight months. That’s when I can really trace it back to.
Do you feel this started because of the stress from taking over that curriculum initiative at work?

I think it started around then, yes… or at least that’s when I can trace it beginning. When I took over the STEM-Arts curriculum initiative, it felt like this big turning point. At first I honestly thought, “Okay, this is just a stressful project, I’m stretched thin, anyone would feel worn out.” So I didn’t really question it.

But over time—maybe because it kept going and didn’t let up—it started to feel like more than ordinary work stress. It’s been building for about eight months now, since that initiative began, and I guess I’ve connected the two because that’s when I first noticed myself pulling away from things I normally cared about. So… yes, the work stress seems like where it started, but it’s also continued in a way I didn’t expect.
If the stress from that work initiative were removed, do you think you would still be feeling this way?

I wish I could say yes, that if the work stress went away I’d just sort of come back online, but… I’m not sure that’s true anymore. The thing that scared me enough to come in is that I don’t feel like myself even when I’m not actively dealing with work.

Like, if I get a free hour, I used to automatically reach for something—my paints, or I’d think about going for a hike, or choir, or Sunday with my family. Those things used to feel like they had some pull. Now I’ll sit there and think, “I could do that,” and then I just… don’t. It’s not even always because I’m busy in that moment. It’s more like I can’t care enough to start.

So maybe the initiative triggered it or made it worse, but if you took it away tomorrow, I’m afraid this blankness would still be there. That’s the part that doesn’t feel like just stress to me.
Have you been feeling down or depressed most days?

Yes… most days, yes. It’s not always like I’m openly crying or anything, though sometimes I do feel like I’m right on the edge of it. It’s more like there’s this heavy gray film over everything, and I’m moving through the day under it.

I can be in the classroom, surrounded by students and noise and all the normal activity, and still feel strangely hollow, like I’m there but not really connected to any of it. And then I’ll go home and be with my husband, and it’s the same thing. I should feel comforted or present, but instead I can feel this sadness sitting in me, and sometimes I’m close to tears for no obvious reason. So… yes, I’d say it’s there most days.
During these past eight months, was there ever a stretch of two months when you felt mostly back to your usual self?

No… I don’t think there was. I’ve been trying to think back, because eight months is long enough that the weeks kind of blur together, but I can’t point to any two-month stretch where I felt mostly like myself again.

It’s been building pretty steadily since I took over that STEM-Arts curriculum initiative. There may have been a day here or there where I thought, “Okay, maybe I’m doing a little better,” or I got through things more smoothly, but not a real sustained period. Not two months of feeling back to normal. It’s more like it’s been there in the background the whole time, and if anything it’s just become more noticeable as the months have gone on.
Do you find yourself worrying excessively about a lot of different things?

I’m not sure I’d call it that, exactly. I mean, I do think about things, but I don’t know if it’s worry in the sense of my mind jumping from one catastrophe to another all day.

It’s more like… I get stuck on how everything feels hard, or whether I’m keeping up, but I’m not sure it’s a bunch of different worries. I don’t really sit there worrying about every possible thing—money, health, family, the house, all of that—at least not in a way that stands out to me.

So… maybe some worry, yes, but I wouldn’t say I’ve noticed excessive worrying about lots of different things. It feels less like nervous worrying and more like being weighed down, if that makes sense.
Before these past eight months, had you already been feeling down or depressed more often than not for at least two years?

No, not for two years. Before this, I had normal ups and downs, I suppose, but I wouldn’t say I was down more often than not for years.

This really feels like it started building about eight months ago, around when I took over the STEM-Arts curriculum initiative. At first I think I told myself it was just stress or adjustment, like I just needed to get used to the new responsibilities, but over time it became more constant. So… no, I wouldn’t say this was already going on for two years before that. It’s more this eight-month stretch that stands out.
Have you been having trouble sleeping?

Yes… definitely. My sleep has been really erratic for months now. Some nights I get into bed exhausted, and then I just lie there awake, going over little details in my head—especially things connected to the grant and the curriculum work, like what I forgot to follow up on or whether something’s going to fall apart.

And then even if I do fall asleep, I’ll often wake up around three or four in the morning. It’s that awful kind of waking up where I’m immediately alert, but not rested—just lying there staring at the ceiling, thinking, “Please, just go back to sleep,” and of course that makes it worse.

There are nights where I technically sleep longer, but it doesn’t feel like good sleep. I get up feeling like I never really rested at all, like I’ve been awake in some part of my brain the whole time. It’s been going on long enough that I almost don’t remember what it feels like to wake up refreshed.
Have these symptoms been making it hard for you to function at work, at home, or with other people?

Yes… it has. I wish I could say I’m still managing the same as before, but I’m really not.

At work it’s been the most obvious. I’ve missed several teaching sessions, which is not like me. I used to be very dependable about showing up, even if I was tired or had a lot going on, and now there have been times where I just couldn’t get myself there or couldn’t face being in front of the students. And I’ve been avoiding some of the student workshops too, partly because they require so much preparation and energy and follow-through, and I just don’t feel like I can keep up with all the responsibilities the way I used to. It’s embarrassing, honestly, because I know people are relying on me.

At home, my husband has had to step in more. Not in some dramatic way every single day, but enough that it’s noticeable. I’ll pull back from family plans or say I can’t go, or I’ll just sort of disappear into myself and leave him to handle things. Sometimes I don’t feel safe pushing through on my own, if that makes sense—not physically unsafe exactly, but like I don’t trust myself to keep functioning and smiling and pretending I’m okay. So yes, it’s affecting work, home, and how I am with people.
Did the work initiative start within three months before these symptoms began?

I think so, yes… or at least it was right around then. The symptoms really started building after I took over the STEM-Arts curriculum initiative, and that’s been about eight months now.

It wasn’t like one exact day where I can say, “That’s when everything changed,” but the timing feels connected. I took on the initiative, and then over the weeks after that I started feeling like I was slipping more and more. So yes, it began within that kind of time frame after the work initiative started.
Have you noticed a significant change in your appetite?

I’m not really sure. I don’t think I’ve noticed a clear, dramatic change in my appetite, at least not in the way people describe where they suddenly can’t eat at all or they’re eating constantly.

It’s more that I haven’t been paying very close attention, honestly. Some days I eat normally, and other days I realize I’ve sort of skipped a meal or just picked at something, but I don’t know if that’s an appetite thing or just being distracted and not having the energy to organize food. I haven’t been tracking my weight or anything like that, so I can’t really say there’s been a significant change.
Have you had thoughts that life isn’t worth living, or thoughts of harming yourself?

Yes… I have. Not like I’ve sat down and made a plan or anything like that, but I have had thoughts that really scare me.

It tends to happen late at night, especially when I’m alone in the studio and everything is quiet and I’m already exhausted. I’ll catch myself thinking that it would be a relief if I just didn’t wake up. And then I almost feel shocked at myself, like, “Why am I thinking that?” because I don’t want to be someone who thinks that way. But it comes up, and it feels very dark and very heavy.

I haven’t made a plan to hurt myself. I want to be clear about that. But the thoughts were frightening enough that I told my husband I couldn’t keep handling them by myself anymore. I didn’t want to be alone with them and pretend they weren’t happening.
Have you been feeling unusually tired or low in energy nearly every day?

I’m not sure how to answer that exactly. I mean… I do feel worn down a lot, but I don’t know if I’d call it unusually tired in a clear medical sense, or whether it’s just life and work and not sleeping well enough or pushing myself too much.

Most days I feel like I’m dragging, but I haven’t really measured it, if that makes sense. Some mornings I can still get up and do what I need to do, but it takes more effort than I think it used to. And then other days I’ll sit there thinking I should be doing something simple, like making lunch or answering an email, and it feels like my body just doesn’t want to start.

So… yes, maybe low energy, but I’m hesitant because I don’t know what counts as “nearly every day” or “unusually.” I just know I haven’t felt like myself, and a lot of things feel heavier than they should.
Have you been feeling worthless or excessively guilty?

Yes… I think so. I don’t know if “worthless” is the word I would have chosen right away, but I do get this really intense feeling that I’m failing people.

It comes up a lot with the curriculum project I’ve been working on. If anything goes wrong — even something small, like a section not being clear enough, or I miss something, or there’s a delay — I start thinking I’m letting the students down. And then it spirals into this much bigger thing, like I’m wasting this opportunity I was given.

My parents sacrificed a lot for me to be able to get an education and have the kind of work where I can contribute to something meaningful. So when I make mistakes, even normal mistakes, I don’t just think, “Oh, I need to fix that.” I think, “You’re wasting what they gave up for you. You’re not doing enough. You’re disappointing everyone.” It feels excessive when I say it out loud, but in the moment it feels very true.
Do these symptoms feel stronger than you would expect from the work stress alone?

I’m not completely sure. Part of me wants to say yes, because it does feel bigger than just being busy or having a hard project. But then another part of me keeps thinking, well, the work really is stressful, and maybe I’m just not handling it well, or maybe I’m making too much of it.

I guess what I can say is that the reaction feels out of proportion sometimes. Like, if it were only the workload, I would expect to feel tired or frustrated or maybe anxious about deadlines. But the way it turns into this whole feeling about who I am as a person, or whether I’m failing everyone… that feels heavier than what the actual work situation would explain.

But I don’t know how to separate it cleanly. The work stress is definitely there, and it seems to set things off, but once it starts, it doesn’t feel like it stays contained to the work itself. It kind of spreads into everything. So… I think yes, probably stronger than I’d expect, but I’m not totally confident saying that.
Before this past eight-month period, had you ever gone through another episode of feeling depressed or losing interest in things for at least two weeks?

I’m honestly not sure. I’ve had hard stretches before, like periods where I was down or overwhelmed, but I don’t know if I can clearly say it was an “episode” in the way you mean, or that it lasted at least two weeks with depression or losing interest.

I think I tend to explain things away at the time — like, “Oh, I’m just tired,” or “work is stressful,” or “this is just a difficult season.” So looking back, it’s a little blurry. I can remember times when I wasn’t myself, but I don’t know if it was the same kind of thing as what’s been happening these past months.

So… I guess my answer is that I don’t really know. Nothing stands out to me clearly enough that I’d feel confident saying yes.
Before this started eight months ago, was there ever a time in your life when you felt depressed or lost interest in things nearly every day for at least two weeks?

I don’t think I can say yes with any confidence. I know you’re asking it more specifically — like not just “have I ever had a bad time,” but depressed or not interested in things nearly every day for two weeks or more — and that’s where I get stuck.

I’ve definitely had difficult periods in my life where I was sad or overwhelmed or not feeling like myself, but I can’t clearly remember a time before these last eight months where it was that steady, almost every day, for at least two weeks. Or at least nothing stands out in a way where I could say, “Yes, that was definitely the same kind of thing.”

Part of the problem is I don’t think I was paying attention in that way before. I would usually explain it as stress or being tired or just needing to get through whatever was going on. So looking back, it’s kind of muddled. But if you’re asking whether I remember a clear earlier stretch like that, I’d have to say no, not clearly.
Did these symptoms begin after the death of someone close to you?

No… I don’t think so. I mean, no one close to me died right before this started, at least not in a way that I would connect to it.

There have been losses in life, of course, and people I’ve worried about, but if you mean did this begin as a reaction to someone close to me passing away, then no, that doesn’t really fit. It wasn’t like there was a funeral or a specific death and then everything changed after that.
Before these last eight months, was there ever a time when a doctor or therapist told you that you were depressed?

Not that I can remember, no. I mean, I’ve talked to doctors before for regular things, and I’ve had conversations where I probably mentioned stress or being tired or overwhelmed, but I don’t remember anyone actually saying, “You’re depressed,” or giving me that as a diagnosis before all of this.

I’ve never really been someone who went in and said, “I think something is wrong emotionally,” so it’s possible I wasn’t even bringing it up clearly enough. But as far as a doctor or therapist specifically telling me I was depressed before these last eight months… no, I don’t think so. Nothing like that stands out.

Yes… definitely. My sleep has been really erratic for months now. Some nights I get into bed exhausted, and then I just lie there awake, going over little details in my head—especially things connected to the grant and the curriculum work, like what I forgot to follow up on or whether something’s going to fall apart.

And then even if I do fall asleep, I’ll often wake up around three or four in the morning. It’s that awful kind of waking up where I’m immediately alert, but not rested—just lying there staring at the ceiling, thinking, “Please, just go back to sleep,” and of course that makes it worse.

There are nights where I technically sleep longer, but it doesn’t feel like good sleep. I get up feeling like I never really rested at all, like I’ve been awake in some part of my brain the whole time. It’s been going on long enough that I almost don’t remember what it feels like to wake up refreshed.

doctor.intent: Differentiate major depressive disorder from adjustment disorder by determining whether the depressive symptoms are causing clinically significant impairment in daily functioning.
doctor.question: Have these symptoms been making it hard for you to function at work, at home, or with other people?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: I've missed several teaching sessions and have been avoiding student workshops because I can't keep up with the responsibilities the way I used to. At home, my husband has had to step in more because I withdraw from family plans and don't feel safe pushing through alone.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the symptoms are interfering with functioning at work, home, or socially, which directly matches functional impairment.

patient.answer:
Yes… it has. I wish I could say I’m still managing the same as before, but I’m really not.

At work it’s been the most obvious. I’ve missed several teaching sessions, which is not like me. I used to be very dependable about showing up, even if I was tired or had a lot going on, and now there have been times where I just couldn’t get myself there or couldn’t face being in front of the students. And I’ve been avoiding some of the student workshops too, partly because they require so much preparation and energy and follow-through, and I just don’t feel like I can keep up with all the responsibilities the way I used to. It’s embarrassing, honestly, because I know people are relying on me.

At home, my husband has had to step in more. Not in some dramatic way every single day, but enough that it’s noticeable. I’ll pull back from family plans or say I can’t go, or I’ll just sort of disappear into myself and leave him to handle things. Sometimes I don’t feel safe pushing through on my own, if that makes sense—not physically unsafe exactly, but like I don’t trust myself to keep functioning and smiling and pretending I’m okay. So yes, it’s affecting work, home, and how I am with people.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there has been a major stressor within the past 3 months, which would support adjustment disorder over major depressive disorder.
doctor.question: Did the work initiative start within three months before these symptoms began?

target_item.name: Duration
target_item.manifestation: This has been building for about 8 months, since I took over the STEM-Arts curriculum initiative.
target_item.reason: The question is asking about the timing of symptom onset in relation to the work initiative, which is covered by the duration/onset profile stating this has been building for about 8 months since taking over the STEM-Arts curriculum initiative.

patient.answer:
I think so, yes… or at least it was right around then. The symptoms really started building after I took over the STEM-Arts curriculum initiative, and that’s been about eight months now.

It wasn’t like one exact day where I can say, “That’s when everything changed,” but the timing feels connected. I took on the initiative, and then over the weeks after that I started feeling like I was slipping more and more. So yes, it began within that kind of time frame after the work initiative started.

doctor.intent: Determine whether this episode meets full major depressive episode criteria rather than adjustment disorder by assessing a key additional depressive symptom.
doctor.question: Have you noticed a significant change in your appetite?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about appetite changes, but the provided symptom profile does not include an appetite or weight-change symptom item.

patient.answer:
I’m not really sure. I don’t think I’ve noticed a clear, dramatic change in my appetite, at least not in the way people describe where they suddenly can’t eat at all or they’re eating constantly.

It’s more that I haven’t been paying very close attention, honestly. Some days I eat normally, and other days I realize I’ve sort of skipped a meal or just picked at something, but I don’t know if that’s an appetite thing or just being distracted and not having the energy to organize food. I haven’t been tracking my weight or anything like that, so I can’t really say there’s been a significant change.

doctor.intent: Assess suicidal ideation to help distinguish major depressive episode severity from adjustment disorder and evaluate safety.
doctor.question: Have you had thoughts that life isn’t worth living, or thoughts of harming yourself?

target_item.name: Death_Suicide
target_item.manifestation: On late nights in the studio I sometimes catch myself thinking it would be a relief if I just didn't wake up, and while I haven't made a plan, those thoughts scare me enough that I told my husband I couldn't keep handling them alone.
target_item.reason: The doctor is directly asking about thoughts that life is not worth living or self-harm, which matches suicidal ideation and thoughts of death.

patient.answer:
Yes… I have. Not like I’ve sat down and made a plan or anything like that, but I have had thoughts that really scare me.

It tends to happen late at night, especially when I’m alone in the studio and everything is quiet and I’m already exhausted. I’ll catch myself thinking that it would be a relief if I just didn’t wake up. And then I almost feel shocked at myself, like, “Why am I thinking that?” because I don’t want to be someone who thinks that way. But it comes up, and it feels very dark and very heavy.

I haven’t made a plan to hurt myself. I want to be clear about that. But the thoughts were frightening enough that I told my husband I couldn’t keep handling them by myself anymore. I didn’t want to be alone with them and pretend they weren’t happening.

doctor.intent: Differentiate a major depressive episode from adjustment disorder by determining whether the patient has low energy/fatigue as an additional core depressive symptom.
doctor.question: Have you been feeling unusually tired or low in energy nearly every day?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about fatigue or low energy nearly every day, but the provided symptom profile does not include a specific fatigue/energy symptom item.

patient.answer:
I’m not sure how to answer that exactly. I mean… I do feel worn down a lot, but I don’t know if I’d call it unusually tired in a clear medical sense, or whether it’s just life and work and not sleeping well enough or pushing myself too much.

Most days I feel like I’m dragging, but I haven’t really measured it, if that makes sense. Some mornings I can still get up and do what I need to do, but it takes more effort than I think it used to. And then other days I’ll sit there thinking I should be doing something simple, like making lunch or answering an email, and it feels like my body just doesn’t want to start.

So… yes, maybe low energy, but I’m hesitant because I don’t know what counts as “nearly every day” or “unusually.” I just know I haven’t felt like myself, and a lot of things feel heavier than they should.

doctor.intent: Differentiate a major depressive episode from adjustment disorder by establishing whether there is pathologic guilt or worthlessness, a core MDD symptom not explained by stress alone.
doctor.question: Have you been feeling worthless or excessively guilty?

target_item.name: Worthlessness_Guilt
target_item.manifestation: When anything goes wrong with the curriculum project, even something small, I keep thinking I'm letting the students down and wasting the sacrifices my parents made for me to have this kind of opportunity.
target_item.reason: The doctor is directly asking about feelings of worthlessness or excessive guilt, which matches this symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Yes… I think so. I don’t know if “worthless” is the word I would have chosen right away, but I do get this really intense feeling that I’m failing people.

It comes up a lot with the curriculum project I’ve been working on. If anything goes wrong — even something small, like a section not being clear enough, or I miss something, or there’s a delay — I start thinking I’m letting the students down. And then it spirals into this much bigger thing, like I’m wasting this opportunity I was given.

My parents sacrificed a lot for me to be able to get an education and have the kind of work where I can contribute to something meaningful. So when I make mistakes, even normal mistakes, I don’t just think, “Oh, I need to fix that.” I think, “You’re wasting what they gave up for you. You’re not doing enough. You’re disappointing everyone.” It feels excessive when I say it out loud, but in the moment it feels very true.

inference.note: Added sufficient depressive symptoms for a major depressive episode (depressed mood, anhedonia, insomnia, guilt/worthlessness, impaired functioning, passive suicidal ideation; likely low energy), making a current severe depressive episode without psychotic symptoms more likely than unspecified depression. Recurrent vs single episode remains unclear because prior episodes have not been assessed. Adjustment disorder remains a differential because symptoms followed a work stressor, but persistence, pervasiveness, and full depressive syndrome argue against it.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the depressive symptoms are clearly in excess of what would be expected from the work stressor, which best distinguishes major depressive disorder from adjustment disorder with depressed mood.
doctor.question: Do these symptoms feel stronger than you would expect from the work stress alone?

target_item.reason: The question asks whether the overall symptoms are disproportionate to work stress alone, but no symptom profile item specifically covers attribution or proportionality to a stressor.

patient.answer:
I’m not completely sure. Part of me wants to say yes, because it does feel bigger than just being busy or having a hard project. But then another part of me keeps thinking, well, the work really is stressful, and maybe I’m just not handling it well, or maybe I’m making too much of it.

I guess what I can say is that the reaction feels out of proportion sometimes. Like, if it were only the workload, I would expect to feel tired or frustrated or maybe anxious about deadlines. But the way it turns into this whole feeling about who I am as a person, or whether I’m failing everyone… that feels heavier than what the actual work situation would explain.

But I don’t know how to separate it cleanly. The work stress is definitely there, and it seems to set things off, but once it starts, it doesn’t feel like it stays contained to the work itself. It kind of spreads into everything. So… I think yes, probably stronger than I’d expect, but I’m not totally confident saying that.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there has been any past depressive episode before this 8-month period, which would distinguish recurrent major depressive disorder (F33.9) from a single current major depressive episode (F32.2) and make adjustment disorder less likely.
doctor.question: Before this past eight-month period, had you ever gone through another episode of feeling depressed or losing interest in things for at least two weeks?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about any prior depressive episodes before the current eight-month period, but the symptom profile only describes current symptoms and duration, not past episode history.

patient.answer:
I’m honestly not sure. I’ve had hard stretches before, like periods where I was down or overwhelmed, but I don’t know if I can clearly say it was an “episode” in the way you mean, or that it lasted at least two weeks with depression or losing interest.

I think I tend to explain things away at the time — like, “Oh, I’m just tired,” or “work is stressful,” or “this is just a difficult season.” So looking back, it’s a little blurry. I can remember times when I wasn’t myself, but I don’t know if it was the same kind of thing as what’s been happening these past months.

So… I guess my answer is that I don’t really know. Nothing stands out to me clearly enough that I’d feel confident saying yes.

doctor.intent: Clarify whether there has ever been a prior depressive episode, which best distinguishes recurrent major depressive disorder from a single episode and adjustment disorder.
doctor.question: Before this started eight months ago, was there ever a time in your life when you felt depressed or lost interest in things nearly every day for at least two weeks?

target_item.reason: The question asks about any prior lifetime episode before the current eight-month period, but the symptom profile only describes the current episode and does not provide information about past depressive episodes.

patient.answer:
I don’t think I can say yes with any confidence. I know you’re asking it more specifically — like not just “have I ever had a bad time,” but depressed or not interested in things nearly every day for two weeks or more — and that’s where I get stuck.

I’ve definitely had difficult periods in my life where I was sad or overwhelmed or not feeling like myself, but I can’t clearly remember a time before these last eight months where it was that steady, almost every day, for at least two weeks. Or at least nothing stands out in a way where I could say, “Yes, that was definitely the same kind of thing.”

Part of the problem is I don’t think I was paying attention in that way before. I would usually explain it as stress or being tired or just needing to get through whatever was going on. So looking back, it’s kind of muddled. But if you’re asking whether I remember a clear earlier stretch like that, I’d have to say no, not clearly.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the depressive symptoms meet the exclusion for adjustment disorder by assessing if they represent a normal bereavement reaction.
doctor.question: Did these symptoms begin after the death of someone close to you?

target_item.reason: The question asks whether the symptoms began after the death of someone close, but the symptom profile does not include bereavement or a death-related trigger; it only notes the symptoms have been building for 8 months since taking over the STEM-Arts curriculum initiative.

patient.answer:
No… I don’t think so. I mean, no one close to me died right before this started, at least not in a way that I would connect to it.

There have been losses in life, of course, and people I’ve worried about, but if you mean did this begin as a reaction to someone close to me passing away, then no, that doesn’t really fit. It wasn’t like there was a funeral or a specific death and then everything changed after that.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there has ever been a prior major depressive episode, which would distinguish recurrent depressive disorder from a single current episode and help separate F33.9 from F32.2/F43.2.
doctor.question: Before these last eight months, was there ever a time when a doctor or therapist told you that you were depressed?

target_item.reason: The question asks about prior professional diagnosis or being told by a doctor/therapist that I was depressed before the current eight-month period, which is not covered by the provided symptom profile items.

patient.answer:
Not that I can remember, no. I mean, I’ve talked to doctors before for regular things, and I’ve had conversations where I probably mentioned stress or being tired or overwhelmed, but I don’t remember anyone actually saying, “You’re depressed,” or giving me that as a diagnosis before all of this.

I’ve never really been someone who went in and said, “I think something is wrong emotionally,” so it’s possible I wasn’t even bringing it up clearly enough. But as far as a doctor or therapist specifically telling me I was depressed before these last eight months… no, I don’t think so. Nothing like that stands out.

opening_question.intent: Learn the patient's main reason for seeking psychiatric care today
opening_question.question: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient meets criteria for a current severe depressive episode without psychotic symptoms: depressed mood most days, marked loss of interest, insomnia, excessive guilt/worthlessness, passive death wishes, and clear functional impairment for about 8 months. Although symptoms began in the context of a work stressor, they are described as persisting beyond and feeling disproportionate to the stressor, favoring a major depressive episode over adjustment disorder. Recurrent depressive disorder is less likely because no prior clearly documented depressive episode was established.
